client: I've been feeling really lost ever since my grandmother passed away last month. It's like this heavy sadness just sits on my chest all day, and I keep finding myself questioning what the point of everything is for me going forward. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I didn't know what else to do.
therapist: The weight in your voice tells me this grief is sitting even deeper than words can quite capture right now — there's a real exhaustion there, like you're carrying something almost too heavy to speak about. I want you to know that showing up here, even when you weren't sure it would help, takes real courage, and that uncertainty you feel makes complete sense after losing someone so important. Can you tell me a little more about your grandmother — what her presence meant in your life?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: She was honestly the one person in my life who I felt truly understood me, like I didn't have to explain myself or perform some version of who I was supposed to be. We'd talk on the phone almost every Sunday, and now when that time rolls around I just stare at my phone and feel this awful hollow feeling. I think part of what makes it so hard is that I'm not sure anyone else in my life will ever know me that way again.
therapist: What you've described — that rare feeling of being truly known without having to perform — is one of the most precious things a relationship can offer, and losing that is a profound loss that goes beyond just missing her presence. The way you talk about those Sunday calls, and now staring at your phone in that silence, really captures how grief can live in the small, ordinary moments just as much as the big ones. I'm curious — when you imagine that kind of deep understanding feeling impossible to find again, is that a thought that feels certain to you, or does some part of you wonder if it might not be the whole truth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, in this moment it feels pretty certain, like I'm not just being dramatic about it. I know logically that people form close relationships all the time, but my grandmother and I had decades of history and she just accepted me in this way that felt almost unconditional, and I don't see how I could build that with someone else. I guess a tiny part of me wonders if I'm closing a door prematurely, but it mostly just feels like the truth right now.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can hold both of those things at once — the pain that feels so certain right now, and that small but honest voice wondering if the door might still be open. That little flicker of doubt isn't weakness or denial; in CBT we'd actually see it as a really important part of you that's worth listening to. What do you think that part of you knows, even in the middle of all this grief, that the more certain part might not be seeing right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think that small part of me knows that my grandmother didn't just appear in my life fully formed, that we built what we had over years of small moments and her choosing to really pay attention to me. But it's hard to hold onto that because it almost makes things feel worse, like the idea of starting over with someone and investing all that time and energy when I'm already so exhausted and lonely. I guess I'm just scared that I don't have it in me right now to try.
therapist: You just said something really wise — that what you and your grandmother had was *built*, not given, and that's a genuinely hopeful insight even though it hurts right now. The exhaustion and fear you're describing makes complete sense; grief takes so much out of us, and the idea of investing in new connections can feel impossible when you're already running on empty. I want to gently reflect back that you don't have to start over *right now* — what would it feel like to give yourself permission to just rest in the grief for a while, without any pressure to rebuild yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That idea sounds nice in theory, but I'm not sure I actually know how to just rest in grief without it turning into something darker, like that questioning what's the point of everything feeling I mentioned. When I give myself too much space to sit with it, my mind tends to spiral into these really bleak places, and then I feel guilty on top of everything else, like I'm not grieving the right way or I'm being self-indulgent. I guess I'm worried that permission to feel it might just mean permission to fall apart.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — there's an urgency there, like this fear of falling apart is very alive in you in this moment, not just something you're describing from a distance. I want to make sure I understand what you mean when you mention things spiraling into bleak places and questioning the point of everything — can you help me understand how dark those places get for you? Your safety matters to me, and I want to make sure we're taking care of that first before anything else.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you asking that directly, and I want to be honest that it's not like I'm thinking about hurting myself or anything like that. It's more like this gray, heavy feeling where I wonder what I'm working toward or what gets me out of bed, not a dangerous place but just a really empty one. I think the guilt comes in because I feel like I should be functioning better than I am, like a month should be enough time to start pulling myself together.
therapist: Thank you for being so honest with me — that takes trust, and I want you to know that what you're describing, that gray emptiness and loss of direction, is a real and valid form of pain even if it isn't dangerous. I also want to gently push back on that "a month should be enough" thought, because grief for someone who was your safest person doesn't run on a timeline, and that belief that you *should* be functioning better sounds like it might be adding a whole extra layer of suffering on top of the grief itself. Where do you think that expectation came from — is that something you'd say to a close friend who had just lost someone so central to their life?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: No, I would never say that to a friend, I'd probably tell them to take all the time they needed and that grief isn't linear or whatever. But it's different when it's me, and I think the expectation comes from this lifelong pattern of feeling like I need to hold it together and not be a burden to people around me. My grandmother was actually one of the only people I felt safe falling apart with, which I guess makes losing her even more complicated than I'd realized until just now.
therapist: What you just uncovered in real time is really significant — that your grandmother wasn't just someone you loved, she was also the one place you felt safe enough to not hold it together, and now that grief and that safe harbor are gone at the same time. There's something in your voice right now that sounds quieter and heavier than your words, like this realization is landing somewhere deep. Can you sit with that for a moment — what does it feel like to recognize that losing her also means losing the one relationship where you didn't have to be strong?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly it feels like a relief and a gut punch at the same time, like I finally have words for why this loss feels so much bigger than just missing her. I think I've been telling myself I'm grieving my grandmother, but I'm also grieving this version of myself that only existed around her, the one who didn't have to be so guarded and exhausted all the time. And now I'm sitting here wondering if that part of me can even exist without her, which is a scary thought to have out loud.
therapist: What you just said — that you're grieving not only her but a version of yourself — is one of the most profound and courageous things you could recognize, and it makes complete sense that it feels like both relief and heartbreak at once. I want to gently offer this: that unguarded, less exhausted part of you didn't only exist *because* of her — she saw it and reflected it back to you, but it was always yours. What would it mean for you to consider that she didn't create that part of you, but rather that she helped you discover it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's a really comforting idea and I want to believe it, but I'm not sure I do yet, because it feels like without her there to reflect it back I just default to the guarded, exhausted version automatically. Like if that unguarded part was really mine, wouldn't I be able to access it on my own sometimes, even just a little? I guess I'm skeptical because the evidence in my daily life right now points more toward it being gone than just hidden.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely fair, and I'd rather you push back on something that doesn't feel true than accept a comforting idea that doesn't actually land. I'm also noticing that even as you're expressing doubt, there's a kind of energy in how you're engaging with this — you're questioning, reasoning, looking for evidence — and I wonder if that very act of examining yourself so carefully is itself a glimpse of that unguarded part, showing up right here in this conversation. Can you think of even one small moment, maybe not recently but at any point, where that less guarded version of you surfaced somewhere other than with her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Actually, there was this one time a few years ago when I was on a hiking trip with a friend and we got a little lost, and instead of panicking I just kind of took charge and we ended up laughing about it for hours around a campfire that night. I remember feeling really present and unself-conscious in a way I almost didn't recognize in myself. But it's hard to connect that person to who I am right now, it feels like a different lifetime.
therapist: That memory is so alive and specific — the laughter, the campfire, that feeling of being fully present — and the fact that you can recall it so vividly tells me that person isn't as far away as she feels right now. I notice that even as you're describing something that sounds almost joyful, there's a kind of wistfulness or distance in how you're telling it, like you're watching it through glass rather than feeling connected to it. What do you think made that moment possible — what was different about that situation that let that unguarded version of you just show up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
